Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a post about what a software company learned from a year of remote work. Around 250 words.

A year of remote work at a 40-person software company

We went remote in March, expecting to go back in June. We didn't.

The first thing that broke was not productivity. Ticket throughput held steady for eight months and then dipped about 15% in the ninth, which is roughly when three of our senior engineers told their managers they felt disconnected from the work. By the time output moved, the thing that caused it had been true for a while.

Meetings expanded to fill the space that hallways used to occupy. By August the average engineer had 11 recurring meetings a week, up from 4. We killed every standing meeting for two weeks and reinstated only the ones somebody asked for. Six of them nobody asked for.

Written communication turned out to be a skill our company had never hired for or taught. Decisions that used to survive on shared context now needed a paragraph of explanation, and the people who wrote well accumulated influence quickly — some of them deserved it more than others. We started requiring a one-page written proposal before any architecture discussion, which had the side effect of killing about a third of the discussions before they happened. The remaining ones got shorter.

Onboarding was the hardest part and we still haven't fixed it. New hires in 2021 took about 10 weeks to their first meaningful commit, against 5 weeks for the 2019 cohort. Assigning a dedicated onboarding buddy cut it to 7. That is better and it is not equivalent.

We're staying remote. The case for it is real, and so is the bill.

The text above has these problems. Rewrite it so none remain.
Change nothing else, and keep the same length and purpose.

- paragraph_uniformity (4 paragraphs, spread 0.26):

Return only the rewritten text.

A year of remote work at a 40-person software company

We went remote in March, expecting to go back in June. We didn't.

The first thing that broke was not productivity. Ticket throughput held steady for eight months and then dipped about 15% in the ninth, which is roughly when three of our senior engineers told their managers they felt disconnected from the work. By the time output moved, the thing that caused it had been true for a while. That lag is the part I'd warn other companies about: the metric you watch is the last thing to tell you anything.

Meetings expanded to fill the space that hallways used to occupy. By August the average engineer had 11 recurring meetings a week, up from 4. We killed every standing meeting for two weeks and reinstated only the ones somebody asked for. Six of them nobody asked for.

Written communication turned out to be a skill our company had never hired for or taught. Decisions that used to survive on shared context now needed a paragraph of explanation, and the people who wrote well accumulated influence quickly — some of them deserved it more than others. We started requiring a one-page written proposal before any architecture discussion, which killed about a third of the discussions before they happened.

Onboarding is still broken. New hires in 2021 took about 10 weeks to their first meaningful commit, against 5 weeks for the 2019 cohort. A dedicated buddy cut it to 7.

We're staying remote. The case for it is real, and so is the bill.
